questions.stem: When sodium chloride dissolves in water, how are the water molecules arranged around the ions?
options: The oxygen end faces Na⁺ ions and the hydrogen end faces Cl⁻ ions
The hydrogen end faces Na⁺ ions and the oxygen end faces Cl⁻ ions
The oxygen end faces both ions, as oxygen is the larger atom
Water molecules bond covalently to each ion to form new molecules
questions.explanation: Water is polar: oxygen carries a partial negative charge and the hydrogen atoms a partial positive charge. The partially negative oxygen is attracted to cations and the partially positive hydrogens to anions, forming ion-dipole attractions, not covalent bonds.

questions.stem: Which bonds and attractions are broken and formed when an ionic solid dissolves in water?
options: Ionic bonds and some hydrogen bonds break; ion-dipole attractions form
Covalent bonds in water break; new ionic bonds form with the solid
Ion-dipole attractions break; ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds form
Only hydrogen bonds break; the ionic bonds stay intact in solution
questions.explanation: The attraction between oppositely charged ions in the lattice must be overcome, and some hydrogen bonds between water molecules break to make room for the ions. Each separated ion is then surrounded by water molecules held by ion-dipole attractions. The covalent bonds within water molecules do not break.

questions.stem: Which equation represents calcium nitrate dissolving in water?
questions.explanation: An ionic compound dissociates into its separate hydrated ions: one Ca²⁺ ion and two nitrate ions, each NO₃⁻. Polyatomic ions such as nitrate stay intact, and the charges must balance.

questions.stem: Using the solubility rules, which compound is insoluble in water?
questions.explanation: Chlorides, bromides and iodides are soluble except with silver and lead(II), so silver bromide is insoluble. Barium chloride and copper(II) chloride are soluble chlorides, and iron(III) sulfate is a soluble sulfate.

questions.stem: Which hydroxide is soluble in water?
questions.explanation: Most hydroxides are insoluble, but those of the group 1 metals and barium are soluble, and calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble. Copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) hydroxides form coloured precipitates.

questions.stem: Barium nitrate solution is added to a solution containing one of these anions. Which anion gives a white precipitate?
questions.explanation: Barium sulfate is insoluble and forms a white precipitate. Barium chloride, barium bromide and barium acetate are all soluble, so no precipitate forms with those anions.

questions.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution of an unknown cation, and an orange-brown precipitate forms. Which cation is present?
questions.explanation: Iron(III) hydroxide is orange-brown (rust coloured). Iron(II) hydroxide is green, copper(II) hydroxide is pale blue, and barium hydroxide is soluble, so Ba²⁺ gives no precipitate.

questions.stem: Silver nitrate solution is mixed with sodium chloride solution. What is the net ionic equation?
questions.explanation: The precipitate is silver chloride, so the net ionic equation shows only the ions that combine to form it. Sodium and nitrate ions are spectator ions, because sodium nitrate is soluble and stays in solution.

questions.stem: Barium chloride solution is mixed with sodium phosphate solution. What is the formula of the precipitate?
questions.explanation: Phosphates are insoluble except with group 1 metals and ammonium, so barium phosphate precipitates. Balancing the charges of Ba²⁺ and PO₄³⁻ needs three barium ions for every two phosphate ions. Sodium chloride is soluble.

questions.stem: Which pair of solutions gives no precipitate when mixed?
questions.explanation: Acetates and chlorides are soluble with these cations, so copper(II) chloride and sodium acetate give only a solution of ions. The other pairs form silver iodide, barium sulfate and iron(III) hydroxide precipitates.

questions.stem: A colourless solution gives a bright yellow precipitate when lead(II) nitrate solution is added. Which anion is most likely present?
questions.explanation: Lead(II) iodide is a distinctive bright yellow solid. Lead(II) chloride and lead(II) sulfate are white, and lead(II) acetate is soluble, so it gives no precipitate.

questions.stem: Before testing a solution for chloride ions with silver nitrate, dilute nitric acid is added. Why?
options: To oxidise the chloride ions so that they react with silver
To remove carbonate ions, which would also precipitate with silver
To provide the nitrate ions needed to form the precipitate
To make silver chloride soluble so that it can be filtered
questions.explanation: Silver carbonate is also insoluble, so carbonate ions would give a false positive. Nitric acid reacts with carbonate to release carbon dioxide, removing it, and adds no interfering ions because nitrates are soluble.

questions.stem: An unknown solution gives an orange-brown precipitate with sodium hydroxide. With barium nitrate it gives a white precipitate that does not dissolve or fizz when dilute nitric acid is added. Which ions are present?
questions.explanation: The orange-brown hydroxide identifies Fe³⁺. Barium carbonate and barium sulfate are both white, but barium carbonate would dissolve with fizzing in acid; the precipitate that stays is barium sulfate, so the anion is sulfate.

questions.stem: Equal volumes of 0.010 mol L⁻¹ calcium nitrate and 0.010 mol L⁻¹ sodium sulfate are mixed, and no precipitate forms, although some lists classify calcium sulfate as insoluble. What best explains this?
options: Calcium sulfate is slightly soluble, so at these concentrations Q is below Ksp
Calcium sulfate is very soluble, so it can never form a precipitate in water
Sodium ions react with the calcium sulfate and keep it dissolved as a complex
The solubility rules apply only to solutions more dilute than 0.010 mol L⁻¹
questions.explanation: Simple rules sort compounds into soluble and insoluble, but some, such as calcium sulfate, are slightly soluble. After mixing, [Ca²⁺] = [SO₄²⁻] = 0.0050 mol L⁻¹, and the ion product is too small to exceed Ksp, so whether a precipitate is seen depends on concentration.

questions.stem: What is the solubility product expression for lead(II) iodide, PbI₂?
questions.explanation: PbI₂(s) ⇌ Pb²⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq), so the iodide concentration is squared because of its coefficient. The solid does not appear in the expression, because the concentration of a pure solid is constant.

questions.stem: What is the solubility product expression for calcium phosphate, Ca₃(PO₄)₂?
questions.explanation: Ca₃(PO₄)₂(s) ⇌ 3Ca²⁺(aq) + 2PO₄³⁻(aq). Each ion concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient, giving cubed calcium and squared phosphate. Coefficients become powers, not multipliers.

questions.stem: Which equation represents the equilibrium in a saturated solution of iron(III) hydroxide?
questions.explanation: In a saturated solution, undissolved solid is in equilibrium with its aqueous ions. Iron(III) hydroxide releases one Fe³⁺ ion and three separate OH⁻ ions; Fe²⁺ would not balance the charge of three hydroxide ions.

questions.stem: Which change alters the value of Ksp for a salt?
questions.explanation: Like any equilibrium constant, Ksp depends only on temperature. Adding solid or stirring does not change the concentrations in a saturated solution, and a common ion lowers the solubility but not Ksp.

questions.stem: At 25 °C, Ksp values are AgCl 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰, AgBr 5.4 × 10⁻¹³ and AgI 8.5 × 10⁻¹⁷. Which salt is least soluble in water?
questions.explanation: All three salts have the same 1 : 1 ratio of ions, so their Ksp values can be compared directly: the smallest Ksp means the lowest solubility. Silver iodide is the least soluble.

questions.stem: Ksp for AgCl is 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ at 25 °C. What is the solubility of AgCl in water in mol L⁻¹?
questions.explanation: If the solubility is s, then [Ag⁺] = [Cl⁻] = s and Ksp = s². So s = √(1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹. The Ksp value itself is not the solubility.

questions.stem: Ksp for PbI₂ is 9.8 × 10⁻⁹ at 25 °C. What is the solubility of PbI₂ in water in mol L⁻¹?
questions.explanation: If the solubility is s, then [Pb²⁺] = s and [I⁻] = 2s, so Ksp = s(2s)² = 4s³. Then s³ = 9.8 × 10⁻⁹ / 4 = 2.45 × 10⁻⁹ and s = 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹. Treating it as a 1 : 1 salt gives 9.9 × 10⁻⁵, and forgetting the factor of 4 gives 2.1 × 10⁻³.

questions.stem: Ksp for Ca(OH)₂ is 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ at 25 °C, and its molar mass is 74.1 g mol⁻¹. What is its solubility in g L⁻¹?
questions.explanation: Ksp = [Ca²⁺][OH⁻]² = s(2s)² = 4s³, so s³ = 1.25 × 10⁻⁶ and s = 1.08 × 10⁻² mol L⁻¹. Multiplying by the molar mass gives 1.08 × 10⁻² × 74.1 = 0.80 g L⁻¹. Leaving the answer in mol L⁻¹ gives 1.1 × 10⁻², and treating Ksp as s² gives 0.17.

questions.stem: A saturated solution of barium sulfate (M = 233.4 g mol⁻¹) contains 2.33 × 10⁻³ g L⁻¹ of dissolved BaSO₄. What is Ksp for BaSO₄?
questions.explanation: The molar solubility is 2.33 × 10⁻³ / 233.4 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹, so [Ba²⁺] = [SO₄²⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ and Ksp = (1.0 × 10⁻⁵)² = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰. Squaring the solubility in g L⁻¹ without converting to mol L⁻¹ gives 5.4 × 10⁻⁶.

questions.stem: The solubility of silver carbonate, Ag₂CO₃, is 1.28 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹ at 25 °C. What is its Ksp?
questions.explanation: Ag₂CO₃(s) ⇌ 2Ag⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq), so [Ag⁺] = 2s and [CO₃²⁻] = s, and Ksp = (2s)²s = 4s³ = 4 × (1.28 × 10⁻⁴)³ = 8.4 × 10⁻¹². Using s³ alone gives 2.1 × 10⁻¹², and treating it as a 1 : 1 salt gives 1.6 × 10⁻⁸.

questions.stem: In a saturated calcium hydroxide solution at 25 °C, [OH⁻] = 0.022 mol L⁻¹. What is Ksp for Ca(OH)₂?
questions.explanation: Each Ca²⁺ ion comes with two OH⁻ ions, so [Ca²⁺] = 0.022/2 = 0.011 mol L⁻¹. Ksp = [Ca²⁺][OH⁻]² = 0.011 × 0.022² = 5.3 × 10⁻⁶. Forgetting to square [OH⁻] gives 2.4 × 10⁻⁴.

questions.stem: At 25 °C, Ksp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ and Ksp(Ag₂CO₃) = 8.4 × 10⁻¹². Which statement about their molar solubilities in water is correct?
options: AgCl is more soluble, because its Ksp is larger
They are equally soluble, because both are silver salts
Ag₂CO₃ is less soluble, because its Ksp is smaller
Ag₂CO₃ is more soluble, even though its Ksp is smaller
questions.explanation: Ksp values can be compared directly only for salts with the same ion ratio. AgCl has s = √Ksp = 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹, while Ag₂CO₃ has 4s³ = Ksp, giving s = 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹, about ten times greater.

questions.stem: After two solutions are mixed, [Ag⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ and [Cl⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹. Ksp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰. What happens?
options: A precipitate forms, because Q = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ is greater than Ksp
No precipitate forms, because Q = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ is less than Ksp
A precipitate forms, because Q = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ is greater than Ksp
No precipitate forms, because the ion concentrations are equal
questions.explanation: The ion product Q = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸, which is greater than 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰, so the solution would be supersaturated and AgCl precipitates until Q falls to Ksp. The concentrations are multiplied, not added.

questions.stem: 50.0 mL of 0.0040 mol L⁻¹ Pb(NO₃)₂ is mixed with 50.0 mL of 0.0040 mol L⁻¹ KI. Ksp(PbI₂) = 9.8 × 10⁻⁹. Does a precipitate form?
options: No, because Q = 8.0 × 10⁻⁹ is less than Ksp
Yes, because Q = 6.4 × 10⁻⁸ is greater than Ksp
Yes, because Q = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ is greater than Ksp
No, because Q = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵ is less than Ksp
questions.explanation: Mixing equal volumes halves each concentration, so [Pb²⁺] = [I⁻] = 0.0020 mol L⁻¹. Q = [Pb²⁺][I⁻]² = 0.0020 × 0.0020² = 8.0 × 10⁻⁹, just below Ksp, so no precipitate forms. Ignoring the dilution gives 6.4 × 10⁻⁸, and forgetting to square [I⁻] gives 4.0 × 10⁻⁶.

questions.stem: Ksp(PbSO₄) = 2.5 × 10⁻⁸ at 25 °C. What is the highest concentration of Pb²⁺ that can remain in solution if [SO₄²⁻] = 0.010 mol L⁻¹?
questions.explanation: At the point of precipitation [Pb²⁺][SO₄²⁻] = Ksp, so [Pb²⁺] = 2.5 × 10⁻⁸ / 0.010 = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ mol L⁻¹. Any higher lead concentration would make Q exceed Ksp. The value 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ is √Ksp, the solubility in pure water.

questions.stem: Ksp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ at 25 °C. What is the solubility of AgCl in 0.10 mol L⁻¹ sodium chloride solution?
questions.explanation: The chloride ions already present come almost entirely from NaCl, so [Cl⁻] = 0.10 mol L⁻¹ and s = [Ag⁺] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ / 0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ mol L⁻¹. This is far less than the solubility in pure water, 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹, because of the common ion.

questions.stem: Potassium iodide is added to a saturated solution of PbI₂ in contact with solid PbI₂. What happens?
options: Nothing changes, because the solution is saturated
Ksp increases, so more PbI₂ can dissolve
questions.explanation: Adding iodide ions raises [I⁻], so Q exceeds Ksp and the equilibrium PbI₂(s) ⇌ Pb²⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) shifts left, precipitating more PbI₂ and lowering [Pb²⁺]. Ksp is unchanged at constant temperature.

questions.stem: Why is the concentration of lead ions in drinking water and soil monitored?
options: Lead ions cause algal blooms by acting as a plant nutrient
Lead is toxic and accumulates in the body, harming the nervous system
Lead ions react with water to release hydrogen gas into homes
Lead ions make water too alkaline for plants and animals
questions.explanation: Lead is a toxic heavy metal that builds up in the body over time and damages the nervous system; young children are especially at risk. Algal blooms are linked to nutrients such as phosphate, not lead.

questions.stem: In a gravimetric analysis, the Pb²⁺ in a water sample is found by adding excess potassium iodide. What is then done to the PbI₂ formed?
options: It is redissolved in water and its volume measured
It is titrated with sodium hydroxide to find the lead
It is heated until it gives off lead gas, which is collected
It is filtered, washed, dried to constant mass and weighed
questions.explanation: Gravimetric analysis converts the analyte into a precipitate of known formula, which is collected, washed to remove soluble impurities and dried until its mass is constant. The amount of lead is then calculated from the mass of PbI₂ and its formula.

questions.stem: In a gravimetric analysis for lead, the iodide solution is added in excess. Why?
options: Excess iodide reacts with the filter paper, so the precipitate is easier to collect
A high [I⁻] dissolves any other precipitates, so only lead iodide remains
A high [I⁻] lowers the solubility of PbI₂, so almost all the lead precipitates
Excess iodide raises Ksp, so the precipitate forms more quickly in the beaker
questions.explanation: With iodide in excess, the common ion effect pushes PbI₂(s) ⇌ Pb²⁺ + 2I⁻ to the left, so the [Pb²⁺] left in solution is tiny and the lead is effectively all collected. Ksp is fixed at a given temperature.

questions.stem: Why is the phosphate concentration of rivers and lakes monitored?
options: Phosphate ions react with dissolved oxygen to form a poisonous gas
Excess phosphate causes algal blooms, which lower dissolved oxygen
Phosphate ions are toxic heavy metals that damage the nervous system
Phosphate ions make the water strongly acidic and dissolve rocks
questions.explanation: Phosphate is a plant nutrient. Run-off from fertilisers, detergents and sewage can cause excessive algal growth (eutrophication), and when the algae die and decompose, dissolved oxygen falls and aquatic life suffers.

questions.stem: Phosphate is removed from waste water by adding Fe³⁺. Ksp(FePO₄) = 9.9 × 10⁻¹⁶. If [Fe³⁺] is kept at 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹, what is the highest [PO₄³⁻] that can remain in solution?
questions.explanation: Ksp = [Fe³⁺][PO₄³⁻], so [PO₄³⁻] = 9.9 × 10⁻¹⁶ / 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 9.9 × 10⁻¹¹ mol L⁻¹. Any phosphate above this precipitates as FePO₄. The value 3.1 × 10⁻⁸ is √Ksp, the solubility in pure water.
